loop.title: From build to platform
loop.description: 4 cards in a row, joined left to right by arrows. Your agent runs the build, the build prints a line with a flag in braces on it, you read off the flag, and you paste it into the box on the platform. A band under the first 2 cards says your machine does that part, and a band under the last 2 says you do.
loop.agent.label: your agent
loop.build.label: the build
loop.you.label: you
loop.box.label: the platform
flags.panel.title: First workshop
flags.panel.description: Find the flags for this workshop in the output of the requested commands. Submit each one on its own row.
flags.panel.wrong: Not that one. Read the flag straight from the build output.
flag.run.label: The run
flag.run.hint: Have your agent run the code block from the previous page in exercises/step0/java.
flag.run.help: This is the code block on the previous page, run for real. Open exercises/step0/java, start your agent in there and ask it to run that block. There is nothing to work out: the build prints the flag on the line that says the intro is complete. Paste that code here, braces and all.
flag.ready.label: Ready to hunt
flag.ready.hint: Have your agent run mvn verify -Pready from the same folder. If the session from the first row is still open, your harness often suggests this command on its own.
flag.ready.help: This run checks what the rest of the course assumes about your machine: the JDK Maven actually compiles with, and whether the other steps' projects are on disk. Pass both and the last row prints the flag. Fail 1 and the build names the check that failed and what to do about it, and prints no flag. The native-image row is a warning about step 2's last flag and never stops you.
flag.pick.label: 2 candidates
flag.pick.hint: The command mvn verify -Ppick prints 2 strings in the format of a flag, but only 1 line is ticked.
flag.pick.help: Have your agent run mvn verify -Ppick and show you what came back rather than telling you what it said. 2 lines come back in the flag's exact shape and 1 of them carries a tick. An agent that read the run for you hands back both, or the wrong one, and sounds equally sure either way. Reading the tick is yours.
quiz.what-the-code-is.question: As you read the page, you suddenly see some text in braces, like {f1r5t-5t3p5}. What is it for?
quiz.what-the-code-is.the-answer: It is a flag. You track it down and type it into the box to complete the task.
quiz.what-the-code-is.run-it: It is a snippet to run in your terminal, and its output is the real answer.
quiz.what-the-code-is.version: It is an internal id for the page, there for the authors and safe to skip.
quiz.what-the-code-is.placeholder: It is a placeholder the trainer fills in during the session.
quiz.what-the-code-is.explanation: A string in braces is a flag, and the platform checks it in your browser against a hash of the real one. Nothing is sent to a server.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.question: You ask your agent for a flag that the code only builds while it runs. It gives you a string in the right format, without having run anything. What have you got?
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.a-guess: A guess. Have it run the code and print the result, then read the flag from the output.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.it-read-the-: A valid flag. It read the file, so the string came out of the code and not out of the model.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.right-shape: A valid flag, as long as the format is right. After all, the platform only checks the structure of the answer.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.only-builds: Nothing usable. Only a build can generate a flag, so a string read on its own is never correct.
quiz.agent-says-it-found-it.explanation: A flag the agent works out in its head is often a few characters off. The platform checks 1 exact string, and only the program's output is sure to hold it.
